title: Database Index
body:
An auxiliary data structure — usually a B-tree — that lets the database find rows matching a value without scanning every row in the table. A card catalog: instead of checking each item on the shelf, you look up the location directly.

Without one, a query filtering on a column does a full table scan, which is fine at a thousand rows and catastrophic at ten million. With one, lookups on that column stay roughly logarithmic. The trade is that every index costs disk space and slows down writes, since each insert, update, and delete must maintain the index too — so you index the columns you actually filter, sort, or [[JOIN]] on, not everything. A [[Primary Key]] is indexed automatically; foreign keys often are not, which is a common cause of slow joins. Indexes are stored and maintained on the database server. See [[SQL]].
